title: Ahead of the Deal: How the United States Can Build an Energy Project Pipeline in Emerging Markets
gist: U.S. development finance keeps failing to move the needle on emerging-market power because every administration funds only late-stage deals that barely exist in poor markets; the fix is to shift toward early-stage venture-style risk, delegated origination via specialized private partners, and public grid/procurement support that unlocks follow-on private investment for American firms.

insights.claim: Each of the past five U.S. presidential administrations launched a high-profile initiative to mobilize private capital into emerging-market power (Obama's Power Africa, Trump's DFC, Biden's PGII and JETPs, and Trump II's MCC energy focus), making overseas electricity infrastructure a durable bipartisan priority.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Overseas energy-infrastructure finance is one of the few U.S. policy areas insulated from partisan reversal, so exposure to it is durable across administrations for firms and allies positioning around it.
insights.quote: each of the past five presidential administrations has launched high-profile initiatives to mobilize private capital for power sector investment in lower-income economies
insights.locator: In an era of otherwise deep political division

insights.claim: Despite five administrations of effort, sub-Saharan Africa's total population without electricity access has stayed largely unchanged since 2010, and Indonesia and South Africa remain heavily coal-dependent for power.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The energy-access market opportunity in these regions remains almost entirely unaddressed after 15 years, signaling the binding constraint is structural, not capital availability.
insights.quote: The total number of people in sub-Saharan Africa without electricity access has remained largely unchanged since 2010.
insights.locator: Yet none of these previous presidential efforts

insights.claim: Since 2020 the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation has approved support for just thirty-eight energy projects in low- and lower-middle-income economies, revealing how thin the executable deal flow has been.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The DFC's low deal count over five years quantifies the pipeline shortage that caps U.S. energy-finance deployment regardless of available capital.
insights.quote: since 2020, the DFC has approved support for just thirty-eight energy projects in low- and lower-middle-income economies
insights.locator: And since 2020, the DFC has approved

insights.claim: U.S. initiatives fail for one shared reason: every administration mobilized private capital by supporting individual deals at the very latest stages of development, a strategy that works in mature markets but fits few emerging markets where projects rarely reach that stage.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The core investable insight is that the constraint is upstream project preparation, not late-stage financing, redirecting where value and policy leverage actually sit.
insights.quote: they all tried to mobilize private capital into energy projects using the same strategy: supporting individual deals at the very latest stages of project development
insights.locator: This paper argues that global U.S. electricity investment

insights.claim: The binding constraint on financing clean energy in developing economies is a lack of well-prepared bankable projects, not a lack of capital, per a 2021 open letter from the Global Infrastructure Facility's network of pension funds, insurers, and banks.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Investors chasing emerging-market energy should target project-preparation capacity, since capital already exceeds the supply of investable deals.
insights.quote: what is holding back delivery of climate-friendly and sustainable infrastructure is not a lack of capital, but a lack of well-prepared projects
insights.locator: The Global Infrastructure Facility's Advisory Partners

insights.claim: Less than 10 percent of infrastructure projects in Africa reach financial close and about 80 percent fail at the feasibility and business-planning stage, so agencies that only fund late-stage deals miss the vast majority of potential projects.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The 80% feasibility-stage failure rate defines exactly where intervention capital and de-risking tools have the highest marginal impact.
insights.quote: Less than 10 percent of infrastructure projects in Africa reach financial close, and about 80 percent fail at the feasibility and business planning stage
insights.locator: In emerging markets, very few projects get that far

insights.claim: Deals touted as U.S. private-capital mobilization often turn out to be consortia of public financiers; Mozambique's Central Termica de Temane gas plant is majority-owned by Globaleq (itself owned by UK and Norwegian DFIs) with the DFC, OPEC Fund, and IFC as co-investors.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Headline mobilization figures may overstate genuine private crowd-in, so treat 'blended finance success' claims skeptically when evaluating the sector.
insights.quote: a seemingly successful example of mobilizing private finance reveals, in actuality, a consortium of public development financiers
insights.locator: Center for Global Development senior fellow Charles Kenny

insights.claim: The vast majority of DFC funding is senior debt disbursed at financial close, and the agency relies on private sponsors bringing it advanced-stage projects, making it a reactive partner unable to originate or shape deals toward U.S. strategic goals.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The DFC's senior-debt-at-close model structurally excludes it from the early-stage value and control that would align investments with foreign policy.
insights.quote: Providing only late-stage support and senior debt makes the U.S. government a reactive partner
insights.locator: This approach also limits the benefits

insights.claim: U.S. early-stage project preparation is tiny: USTDA supported 60 power-sector feasibility studies over FY2020-2025 at ~$14.4M/year, the DFC obligated $11.7M for just five power projects in FY2024, and USAID (a historic provider of early-stage grants) no longer exists.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The collapse of upstream U.S. grant capacity, especially USAID's dismantling, leaves a widening origination gap that private and allied partners will need to fill.
insights.quote: the USTDA supported a total of sixty feasibility studies in the power sector globally, obligating an average of just $14.4 million each year
insights.locator: The Early-Stage Support That Exists Is Too Small

insights.claim: Onerous, duplicative DFC project reviews, sometimes re-doing assessments already completed by IFC-aligned peer institutions, impose a de facto cap on U.S. investment scale and disadvantage all Western financiers versus faster Chinese lenders.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Procedural slowness is a competitive liability in great-power infrastructure competition, so speed reforms (or their absence) directly affect who wins emerging-market energy tenders.
insights.quote: a contract that would take five years to discuss, negotiate and sign with the World Bank takes three months when we have dealt with Chinese authorities
insights.locator: The Review Process Is Too Inefficient to Compete

insights.claim: The DFC should deploy early-stage support as an investment rather than a grant, using a SAFE-style instrument (Y Combinator's simple agreement for future equity) that converts to discounted equity at a later trigger, giving the agency upside and staff incentive to hunt early-stage energy projects.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Importing venture-capital mechanics into development finance is the author's central instrument recommendation and would reshape how upstream emerging-market energy capital is structured.
insights.quote: This is analogous to venture capital investing, something U.S. capital markets are quite good at.
insights.locator: Recommendation 1: Deploy Early-Stage Project Support Like an Investment

insights.claim: Elemental Impact already deploys a development-finance SAFE variant, the D-SAFE, with a redemption clause letting it act as a loan or convert to equity for first-of-a-kind clean-energy projects, and as of August 2026 the DFC is exploring this type of solution though it is not yet implemented.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The D-SAFE is a live, watchable template for how early-stage climate-tech de-risking gets structured, with DFC adoption a near-term catalyst to track.
insights.quote: As of August 2026, the DFC is exploring this type of solution, though it has not yet been fully developed or implemented.
insights.locator: This mechanism is already being deployed

insights.claim: The DFC provides no concessional (below-market) capital even in poor countries, a self-imposed constraint rooted in OPIC-era culture rather than statute, since the requirement to exceed costs each year no longer exists.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Because the barrier is cultural not legal, a concessional window could be created without legislation, an under-priced policy option that could unlock riskier high-impact deals.
insights.quote: Many of the driving forces behind this approach are historical and cultural, rather than statutory.
insights.locator: Recommendation 2: Create a Concessional Finance Window

insights.claim: The author proposes a dedicated DFC concessional finance window for high-risk high-impact projects, citing the U.S. Export-Import Bank's China and Transformational Exports Program as precedent for a special streamlined window to counter Chinese competition in strategic sectors.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: A concessional carve-out reframes the recurring 'development vs. returns' fight and would expand the set of financeable frontier-market energy projects.
insights.quote: Carving out a concessional window would help guarantee it can do both.
insights.locator: Recommendation 2: Create a Concessional Finance Window

insights.claim: The DFC lacks meaningful overseas presence and internal technical expertise in emerging energy technologies and critical minerals, a gap widened by USAID mission closures, so it should delegate project origination to specialized external partners.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Specialized funds and technical firms that can originate and de-risk projects become the strategic intermediaries the U.S. government must rely on, a role worth positioning for.
insights.quote: The DFC lacks a significant overseas presence, which limits its capacity to proactively identify promising early-stage projects.
insights.locator: Delegate Origination to External Partners

insights.claim: The Orion Critical Mineral Consortium, a bespoke fund with the mining firm Orion Resource Partners investing in strategic critical-minerals projects in DFC-eligible markets, is a template where the U.S. provides capital and the private partner provides sector expertise the DFC lacks.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The Orion model signals the U.S. government's preferred vehicle structure for critical-minerals and energy origination, a partnership form specialized investors can replicate.
insights.quote: The Orion Critical Mineral Consortium is a bespoke fund designed to invest in strategic critical minerals projects in DFC-eligible markets.
insights.locator: Recommendation 3: Empower External Entities

insights.claim: The DFC's 2025 reauthorization already grants authority to create government-owned 'special projects' companies and partnerships, and it is exploring a joint venture with Armenia's government to develop a transit corridor including electricity transmission.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The statutory authority already exists, so government-owned development companies could scale quickly without new legislation; the Armenia JV is an early live example to watch.
insights.quote: This would require no statutory change
insights.locator: Recommendation 3: Empower External Entities

insights.claim: The DFC should provide corporate loans to trusted companies building diversified project pipelines rather than only financing standalone projects, and is currently considering a corporate loan for multiple electricity generation and distribution projects in Greece and Romania.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Corporate-level lending shifts DFC risk assessment from projects to sponsors and reduces review burden, a structural move that favors well-capitalized multi-project developers.
insights.quote: the DFC is currently considering a corporate loan for the development, construction, commissioning, and operation of multiple electricity generation and distribution projects in Greece and Romania
insights.locator: Recommendation 4: Provide Corporate Loans

insights.claim: More than 80 percent of energy infrastructure in developing markets is public, so a U.S. strategy focused almost exclusively on private-sector transactions omits by definition the foundational grid and transmission infrastructure that enables follow-on private generation investment.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Public grid strength is the true unlock for private generation deals, reframing where catalytic capital should be aimed to enable downstream investment.
insights.quote: more than 80 percent of energy infrastructure in developing markets is public
insights.locator: Build Market Opportunities by Prioritizing Grid Systems

insights.claim: The DFC's 2025 reauthorization requires it to develop guidelines for supporting state-owned enterprises, sovereign wealth funds, and parastatals, but no such policy has yet been made public, opening a path to invest in public grids, hydropower dams, and nuclear power.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: A forthcoming DFC state-owned-enterprise policy would newly open sovereign grid, hydro, and nuclear assets to U.S. financing, a regulatory catalyst to monitor.
insights.quote: opening the door to investments in public assets and companies, but no such DFC policy has yet been made public
insights.locator: Recommendation 5: Create a DFC Policy for Investing in State-Owned Enterprises

insights.claim: The Millennium Challenge Corporation, with an $830 million FY2026 budget and a portfolio now predominantly energy-focused after the Trump foreign-assistance review, should have its energy portfolio roughly doubled to fund the public grid infrastructure that unlocks follow-on DFC and private generation investment.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: The MCC is an underappreciated grid-funding lever with protected bipartisan support; a doubled energy portfolio would materially expand upstream public-infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: The administration should work with Congress to roughly double the MCC's energy portfolio
insights.locator: Recommendation 6: Double the MCC's Energy Portfolio

insights.claim: Targeted U.S. technical assistance to modernize procurement in ten to twelve emerging markets could let American firms compete for an estimated $20-$30 billion in tenders over five years, per energy-infrastructure security expert Steven Burns.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Procurement-design assistance is a low-cost lever with a quantified commercial payoff for U.S. energy exporters, defining a concrete addressable tender opportunity.
insights.quote: potentially $20–$30 billion over five years, based on the typical annual infrastructure procurement volumes of major emerging markets
insights.locator: Recommendation 7: Target Technical Assistance at Procurement

insights.claim: The author argues most of the reforms need no statutory change because U.S. agencies already have the tools and authorities; what must change is officials' thinking about timing, risk, and how much direct control they retain over investments.
insights.speaker: Katie Auth
insights.so_what: Because implementation hinges on administrative will rather than legislation, these shifts could arrive faster than typical policy change, compressing the timeline for the sector's reorientation.
insights.quote: huge improvements can be made without statutory reform or a wholesale reinvention of existing agencies
insights.locator: Generally, relevant U.S. agencies already have the tools
